verdicts.reason: All seven quotes were found: Panigrahi leaf 41 ('first or second part of the seventh century A.D., which should also be taken to be the date of the ParaSuramesvara temple'), leaf 67 ('c. a.d. 650') and leaf 38 (Banerji: 'cannot be earlier than the eighth century A.D.'); Brown leaf 213 ('towards the end of the eighth century') and leaf 11 (plate list 'c. 8th CENTURY A.D.'); Mitra leaf 192 ('I take the temple to be of the 9th century'); Fergusson leaf 429 ('A D 450, instead of A d 500'). NOTE FOR THE ORCHESTRATOR: 'c. A.D. 650' appears verbatim in Panigrahi 1961 at scan leaves 67, 80 and 175, so it is Panigrahi's own figure, not only the report's. RULING: every date is stylistic or palaeographic, and no foundation inscription is known. The scholars disagree, so the tier is uncertain and no view is chosen. The display value 'c. 7th–8th century CE (debated)' covers the two modern views without making up a range. The note names all five views. Brown also says the shrine 'may have been a subsequent addition' to the hall (leaf 213), which is added to the note.
verdicts.revised_text: Scholars disagree about when it was built. K.C. Panigrahi dated it to about 650 CE. Percy Brown dated it towards the end of the 8th century CE. Older writers gave dates from about 500 CE (Fergusson) to the 9th century CE (Mitra).

verdicts.revised_text: Panigrahi placed it in the time of the Shailodbhava kings, who then ruled the Bhubaneswar area. But he wrote that we do not know whether any of them built temples here.

verdicts.reason: Brown leaf 213 was found: 'the entire length of the two being only 48 feet, while the sikhara of the former is but 44 feet high.' HEIGHT RULING: I collected every figure. (a) Brown 1959: tower 44 ft (13.41 m), and shrine plus hall 48 ft long. (b) Fergusson 1876: plan 'only 20 ft square', which is not a height. (c) Panigrahi 1961: no figure. Leaf 66 only says the ruined Satrughnesvara core stands 'almost to the same height as that of the Parasuramesvara'. The '34½ feet' at leaf 107 belongs to the Mukteshvara, not this temple. (d) Mitra 1880: the entry opening on leaf 191 could not be retrieved in three more queries, so any figure there is unseen. (e) Wikipedia's 40.25 ft is not an accepted source and was not used. There is no ASI measurement. So one accepted figure exists, and no accepted source contradicts it. Unlike Lingaraja, with its 39–55 m spread, there is no disagreement between accepted sources. It is still a single source and not measured by ASI. So it is published attributed to Brown, tier uncertain, as 'about 13 m (44 ft)' with value_m 13.4. sections.size.height_m = 13.4, as the schema requires it to equal value_m. If the orchestrator wants no computed size comparison from a single unmeasured figure, it can set both to null; I would not object.
verdicts.revised_text: Percy Brown gave the height of its tower as about 13 m (44 ft).

verdicts.revised_text: Panigrahi wrote that this temple was built in the same way as the ruined Satrughnesvara temple. There, a hollow corbelled arch (stones stepped inwards) shows above the doorway. He explained that it kept weight off the stone beams over the door.

verdicts.revised_text: On the shrine doorway is a carved slab of planet gods, with their names inscribed beside them. Panigrahi noted that early temples like this one leave out Ketu, the ninth planet. Later temples such as Mukteshvara include him.
